name: Executive order of August 3, 1878 restoring a portion of the Tule River reservation to the public domain
citation: Executive order of August 3, 1878 (signed R. B. Hayes)
nations: Tule River Indian Tribe (Yokuts, with Owens Valley Paiute and Tübatulabal members)
Bands Royce lists as King's River, Owen's River and Tule River Indians
promises: Not a treaty: President Hayes restored to the public domain the part of the Tule River reservation inside boundaries drawn along mountain ridges and survey lines; the order states no acreage and no reason.
It reduced the reservation set apart by executive order of October 3, 1873. There was no agreement with the Tribe and no payment.

breaches.what: The Tule River Tribe says President Hayes's 1878 order cut the reservation back to about its original size and that the President lacked authority under federal law to reduce it; it also says its people on the Madden Farm were forcibly and violently removed to the new reservation in 1876, and claims damages for the 1873 removal and the 1878 reduction.

source.publisher: Native American Rights Fund, National Indian Law Library

breaches.quote: The President lacked the authority under federal law to reduced the size of the Reservation.

landTaken: Royce area 607. The Tribe says the order cut the reservation back to about its original size; it gives the 1873 reservation as 91,837 acres and the present one as 55,396 acres.
compensation: Nothing paid was found. In 2013 the Tribe put its historical damages for the 1878 reduction at $41.9 million in 2007 dollars; this is the Tribe's claim, not an award.
today: The present Tule River Reservation is 55,396 acres by the Tribe's 2013 count. A bill to ratify the Tribe's 2007 water settlement, S. 689, was reported in the Senate on May 12, 2025; it would have the Tribe waive claims related to the creation or reduction of the Reservation. No record of its enactment was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its first reservation of valley farmland (the Madden Farm) was taken by Indian agents through state patents, that its people were forcibly removed to the mountain reservation in 1876, and that the 1878 reduction was beyond the President's authority.

openQuestions: Royce numbers area 607 under the executive order of August 3, 1878: it is the land that order restored to the public domain, partly from the January 9, 1873 reserve and partly from the October 3, 1873 additions. treaties.json gives area 607 to the January 9, 1873, October 3, 1873 and August 3, 1878 entries, and cession-1873-10-03-king-s-river-owen-s-river-tule-river is a second entry for the October 3, 1873 order. Not edited.

Decision for Jordan: the 1878 reduction took back land set apart by executive order, not by treaty. Without a court or Commission finding it stays contested, resting on the Tribe's statement that the President lacked authority.
The acreages (48,000 and 91,837 acres in 1873, 55,396 today) come from the Tribe's 2013 presentation, not the orders; the 1878 order states no acreage.
The Indians of California claims (ICC Dockets 31 and 37) covered aboriginal California land generally and were not reviewed for this file.
The Tribe's own website was not found; its 2016 Senate testimony would not download.
treaties.json lists Big Sandy and North Fork Mono rancherias as present-day tribes; their link to this reservation was not checked.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. In 1878 President Hayes returned part of the Tule River reservation to the public domain, with no agreement and no payment.
plain.happened: The Tule River Tribe says the order cut the reservation back to about its first size and that the President had no authority to shrink it. No court or claims commission finding was found.
plain.today: The Tribe counts 55,396 acres today. Nothing paid or returned was found; a 2025 Senate bill would have the Tribe waive claims over the reduction as part of a water settlement, and had not become law.
